t: The Upanishads are the latest layer of the Vedas and turn from ritual toward questions of the self (Atman) and ultimate reality (Brahman).
They hold a plurality of ideas: some are described as monistic, others, such as the Katha, as dualistic, and later Vedanta schools read them in divergent ways.
Scholars give only broad dates, from about 800 to 300 BCE for the principal texts, and new texts called Upanishads went on being composed into the early modern era.
dyk: In 1656 Dara Shukoh produced the Sirr-i-Akbar, a Persian translation of 50 Upanishads; a Latin version made from a Persian manuscript was published in 1801 and 1802, and Schopenhauer kept a copy by his side.
ev: Olivelle places the Brihadaranyaka and Chandogya Upanishads, the two earliest, in these centuries, give or take a century or so
The prose Upanishads Taittiriya, Aitareya and Kausitaki follow, in Olivelle's chronology
Badarayana's Brahmasutra synthesises the differing accounts of Atman and Brahman
Shankara develops the Advaita ideas of Gaudapada and comments on 11 mukhya Upanishads
Dara Shukoh's Sirr-i-Akbar translates 50 Upanishads from Sanskrit into Persian
Anquetil-Duperron publishes his Latin translation, Oupnek'hat, in two volumes (1801 to 1802)
Max Müller's first volume begins the first systematic English treatment of the 12 principal Upanishads
Yeats and Shri Purohit Swami publish The Ten Principal Upanishads

f.made: Mostly anonymous; teachings are attributed to sages such as Yajnavalkya, Uddalaka Aruni and Shvetaketu, and the Shvetashvatara names its own author; scholars regard the existing texts as the work of many authors
f.form: Sanskrit texts, in prose and verse; 108 are listed in the Muktika canon, of which the first dozen or so, the mukhya (principal) Upanishads, are the oldest
f.where: Embedded in the Brahmanas and Aranyakas of the four Vedas; manuscripts of the 108 with Brahma-Yogin's commentary are held at the Adyar Library
f.known: Atman and Brahman; the doctrine of karma; moksha (liberation); one of the earliest declarations of ahimsa; the Mahavakyas such as Tat tvam asi; a basis for the schools of Vedanta; Persian, Latin and English translations
